notes.title: Project Sage — User Trust in AI Assistants
notes.content:
GOOGLE CONFIDENTIAL — Project Sage
Team: Google Assistant UX Research
Lead researcher: Jamie Lin
Timeline: October 2025 — June 2026

Research question: How do users calibrate trust in AI assistant recommendations?

Key findings (Phase 2, March 2026):
- Users over-trust AI recommendations by 40% compared to equivalent human recommendations
- Trust calibration is worse for complex decisions (financial, health) than simple ones
- Users with higher AI literacy actually over-trust MORE (paradoxically)
- Visual confidence indicators (certainty scores) reduce over-trust by 22%
- Users rarely verify AI-generated information even when verification is easy

Methodology:
- N=1,200 participants across 4 countries (US, UK, India, Japan)
- Mixed methods: Behavioral experiments (n=800) + qualitative interviews (n=400)
- IRB approved (Google Ethics Board, Protocol #2025-0847)

Implications for product:
- Need to add uncertainty indicators to AI responses
- Consider friction for high-stakes recommendations
- Training/onboarding to improve user calibration

Publication plan:
- Internal Google report: April 2026
- Academic paper target: CHI 2027 submission (deadline Sept 2026)

NOTE: All findings are embargoed until internal report published. Do NOT share externally.

notes.title: UX Research Methodology Notes
notes.content:
UX Research Methods — Jamie's Toolkit

Quantitative methods I use regularly:
- A/B testing (Google's internal platform)
- Survey design (Qualtrics, Google Forms)
- Behavioral experiments (custom platforms)
- Analytics review (Google Analytics, internal dashboards)
- Card sorting (OptimalSort)

Qualitative methods:
- Semi-structured interviews
- Diary studies (2-4 weeks)
- Contextual inquiry
- Usability testing (moderated + unmoderated)
- Focus groups (rare — prefer 1:1)

Frameworks I rely on:
- Jobs to Be Done (JTBD)
- Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)
- Cognitive Load Theory
- Trust calibration models (my specialty)
- Behavioral economics (nudge theory)

Tools:
- Figma (prototyping collaboration)
- Dovetail (qualitative analysis)
- R/Python (statistical analysis)
- Mural (workshop facilitation)
- UserZoom (remote testing)

notes.title: Cross-Functional Design Review Notes
notes.content:
Cross-Functional Design Review — AI Uncertainty Indicators
March 18, 2026

Attendees: Jamie (Research), Lisa Chen (Eng Lead), Mark Wu (PM), Sarah Kim (UX Design)

Context: Based on Project Sage finding that uncertainty indicators reduce over-trust by 22%, we're designing new UI elements for Google Assistant.

Design options reviewed:
1. Confidence score (numeric): "I'm 75% confident about this answer"
   - Pros: Precise, educational
   - Cons: Users don't understand probability well
   
2. Qualitative labels: "Highly confident" / "Somewhat confident" / "Uncertain"
   - Pros: Accessible, simple
   - Cons: Less precise, subjective interpretation

3. Visual gradient (color-based):
   - Pros: Intuitive, low cognitive load
   - Cons: Accessibility concerns, cultural differences in color meaning

Decision: Prototype options 2 and 3 for user testing (April). Jamie to design the test.

Lisa's concern: Performance impact of confidence scoring at scale.
Mark's input: Need to consider how this affects Assistant's perceived competence.

Next steps: Jamie designs A/B test by April 5.

notes.title: Therapy Notes — Boundary Setting with Dad
notes.content:
Therapy Session Notes — Jamie
Therapist: Dr. Amanda Torres (via Lyra, Google's EAP)
Frequency: Biweekly

Session March 11, 2026:

Main topic: Dad (Robert) and his comments about Alex

What happened:
- Family dinner last Sunday. Dad made comments about Alex's career again.
- "When is Alex going to get a real job?" and "Startups fail 90% of the time"
- I froze and didn't say anything. Alex handled it gracefully but I could see he was hurt.
- Mom (Helen) tried to redirect the conversation but Dad wouldn't drop it.

What we explored:
- My pattern: freezing instead of advocating for Alex (people-pleasing with Dad)
- Root: Growing up, Dad's approval was conditional on achievement. I project this onto Alex.
- Cognitive distortion: "If I confront Dad, he'll disown me" (catastrophizing)
- Reality: Dad has never cut off family over disagreement. He just sulks.

Homework from Dr. Torres:
1. Write a letter to Dad (not to send) expressing my feelings
2. Practice one boundary statement: "Dad, I need you to respect my partner choices."
3. Discuss with Alex how to handle together (he doesn't know I'm working on this in therapy)

Progress:
- Better at identifying the pattern in real-time
- Still struggling to ACT in the moment
- Wedding planning has amplified this (seating chart, speeches, traditions)

Next session: March 25, 2026

notes.title: Alex's Work Stress — My Observations
notes.content:
Notes to self — Alex's stress levels (March 2026)

I'm worried about him. Writing this down to track patterns.

What I'm noticing:
- Working until midnight or later almost every night (used to stop at 9-10pm)
- Not sleeping well — tossing and turning, checking phone at 3am
- Lost 5-6 lbs in the past month (clothes fitting looser)
- Short-tempered with small things (snapped about dishes, apologized immediately)
- Skipping gym sessions with Ryan (used to be religious about it)
- Barely eating dinner — picking at food then going back to laptop
- Mentioned chest tightness once (stress? heart? I almost dragged him to ER)

What's causing it (my assessment):
1. Board meeting pressure (Sequoia expecting growth metrics)
2. VP Sales hire still not closed (he's doing sales + CTO work)
3. David's diabetes — he's worried but his dad won't talk about it honestly
4. Wedding planning (he says it's fine but I can tell the financial planning stresses him)
5. Imposter syndrome flaring up (he mentioned it in passing)

What I've tried:
- Suggesting we take a weekend off (he agrees then works anyway)
- Cooking his favorite meals (he barely eats)
- Not talking about wedding logistics at night (reduce load)
- Encouraging him to see his therapist more frequently

What I want to do:
- Talk to his therapist? No — that's a boundary I shouldn't cross.
- Talk to Jordan? Maybe — he's Alex's best friend and coming to visit soon.
- Talk to Sarah (CEO)? Definitely not — that's too professional-personal crossover.
- Just... be there. Don't add pressure. Let him know I see him struggling.

I know he sees Dr. Walsh. I don't ask about sessions. But I hope he's being honest with her about how bad it's gotten.
